title: False Claims and Documentation Integrity

sections.learningObjectives:
- Explain key false claims concepts, including the False Claims Act, what makes a claim false, and the consequences of submitting false claims to federal programs.
- Describe documentation integrity and the practices that keep medical records accurate, complete, timely, and trustworthy.
- Recognize that falsifying, altering, backdating, or fabricating medical records or claims is fraud.
- Apply correct procedures when documentation is missing, inaccurate, or a request to falsify is received, including escalating through proper channels.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

A false claim is like turning in a receipt that says you bought something you never actually bought, just to get money back. It is pretending something happened so someone will pay for it.

### Question 2

The False Claims Act is like a big rule that says you cannot ask the government to pay for something that is not true. If you do, there are serious consequences.

### Question 3

A claim is like the bill you hand to someone asking them to pay you back. It lists what you say happened and asks for money in return.

### Question 4

If you did your homework but never wrote it down and never turned it in, the teacher has no proof you did it. In healthcare, if it is not written in the record, there is no proof it happened.

### Question 5

Documentation integrity means the health record tells the real, complete story of the visit, like an honest diary that anyone who needs to can read and trust.

### Question 6

Making up or changing a health record on purpose is lying, and in healthcare lying on a record is a serious crime, not a small mistake.

### Question 7

The False Claims Act is about protecting the government's money, like Medicare and Medicaid, so those programs only pay for care that truly happened.

### Question 8

The paper record has to match the true story of the visit. If the record and the bill tell different stories, something is wrong.

### Question 9

A good record is like a clear, complete, and honest diary entry: true, written at the time, easy to read, and signed so everyone knows who wrote it.

### Question 10

If you write your name on a test, you are responsible for the answers on it. In the same way, the person who types a note into the record is responsible for it being true.

### Question 11

Writing down that a service happened when it did not is like writing a lie in your diary and then using it to get something you do not deserve.

### Question 12

An audit trail is like a security camera on the record: it keeps a list of who opened it and what they changed, so nothing can be altered secretly.

### Question 13

Writing down what happened right away is like writing a note while it is still fresh instead of trying to remember it a month later — the sooner you write it, the more true it is.

### Question 14

If a note is messy and no one can read it, it is like a recipe with smudged writing — nobody can tell what was really done.

### Question 15

'Knowingly' in this law is like three ways of being dishonest: knowing it is a lie, closing your eyes so you do not have to find out it is a lie, or being careless about whether it is true.

### Question 16

Even if you change a typed date to look earlier, the computer keeps a hidden clock that remembers the real time you typed it — like a camera that catches the true story.

### Question 17

Telling the truth in the record protects everyone — the patient gets the right care, and the office stays out of legal trouble, like keeping an honest receipt book for a store.

### Question 18

A medical record is like an official report card for a patient's health — a formal document that can be shown to courts and insurers to prove what happened.

### Question 19

Backdating is like writing today's homework and writing yesterday's date on it so it looks like you finished on time — it makes the record tell a lie about when something happened.

### Question 20

Before asking to be paid, you check that your receipt matches what you actually bought — the record has to back up the bill.

### Question 21

If the bill and the receipt do not match, the right move is to stop and tell the person in charge, not to fix the receipt by making things up.

### Question 22

An honest error is like a typo you fix right away; fraud is like deliberately writing down a false number to trick someone into paying.

### Question 23

If someone cheats the government, the law can make them pay back three times what they took plus extra fines — a very expensive mistake.

### Question 24

A whistleblower is like a teammate who sees cheating and tells the referee; the law lets that person step in and, if the team wins back money, share in the reward.

### Question 25

Charging Medicare for a service that never happened is like charging a customer for a meal you never served.

### Question 26

Authentication is like signing your name at the bottom of your work so everyone knows it was you and that you stand behind it.

### Question 27

If nobody actually used the scale or ruler, writing down numbers is like making up a test score instead of taking the test.

### Question 28

Copy-paste is like reusing an old answer for a new question without checking if the answer still fits — it can be wrong for the new situation.

### Question 29

If you forgot to write a note and add it later, you write 'added later' with today's date instead of pretending you wrote it back then.

### Question 30

If a store gives you too much change, keeping it when you know it is a mistake is still wrong — you should give it back.

### Question 31

The record is like the recipe, and the code is the label on the box — the label has to match what is really in the recipe, not the other way around.

### Question 32

Signing someone else's work as if you did it is like putting your name on a test your friend took — you are claiming something that is not true.

### Question 33

Deliberate ignorance is like covering your eyes and ears so you can say you did not see a problem — the law does not let you escape responsibility that way.

### Question 34

Charging for a large pizza when the receipt shows you ordered a small one is overcharging, even if nobody complains about it.

### Question 35

Fixing a record after being caught to make it look right is like changing your answers after the test is graded and claiming that is what you wrote all along.

### Question 36

If a teacher's note is hard to read, you ask the teacher what it says instead of making up an answer.

### Question 37

Because a health record is an official document, lying in it is like lying in court — it can bring big punishments for anyone who does it.

### Question 38

Write down only what you actually saw or did, like a referee calling only the plays they really saw.

### Question 39

If you see someone taking money they should not take, you tell the person in charge instead of pretending you did not see it.

### Question 40

A reverse false claim is like finding money in your account that is not yours and quietly keeping it instead of giving it back.

### Question 41

Using someone else's log-in is like signing someone else's name on a check — it makes the record say the wrong person did it.

### Question 42

Your job is to write down the true facts and ask for help when you are not sure, like a careful note-taker who checks before writing.

### Question 43

Forging a signature to get paid is clearly lying on purpose for money, which is different from fixing a typo or asking a question.

### Question 44

Material means the lie was big enough to matter — like a wrong number that could change whether someone pays, not a tiny typo that changes nothing.

### Question 45

Even if the boss asks, writing down that something happened when it did not is still lying, and you have to say no and tell someone.

### Question 46

Medical necessity is like showing why you really needed the medicine — the note explains the reason, not just that it was given.

### Question 47

Fixing a mistake is fine, but you do it the right way: cross it out, note the correction, and date it — like a teacher correcting a grade with a note instead of erasing it secretly.

### Question 48

Fraud is lying on purpose to get money; abuse is more like doing things the wrong way without necessarily meaning to cheat.

### Question 49

A false claim is about a lie that changes the money decision, not a tiny typo that changes nothing.

### Question 50

Before sending the bill, you check that every item on it matches something in the chart — like checking your receipt against your shopping bag.

### Question 51

You can get in trouble not only for lying on purpose but also for being so careless about the truth that you should have known it was false.

### Question 52

When someone asks to see your records, you show them the real ones you have — you do not make up new ones to fill the gaps.

### Question 53

Having one clear way to fix mistakes is like a school rule for fixing grades — everyone does it the same honest way so nothing looks sneaky.

### Question 54

If you see a wrong label on a patient's chart, you point it out to the person who can fix it properly instead of ripping it off or leaving it.

### Question 55

The assistant writes down the facts they see and do, but the doctor or coder makes the big clinical and code decisions — like a scorekeeper recording the game without making the referee's calls.

### Question 56

If everyone on a team cheats, it is still cheating — you tell the coach instead of joining in.

### Question 57

Write down the numbers the thermometer and cuff really showed — not made-up numbers that sound about right.

### Question 58

The code is the label, and the record is the real thing — the label has to match the real thing, not the real thing change to fit a label.

### Question 59

If the bill does not match the receipt, you fix the bill to match what really happened — you do not rewrite the receipt.

### Question 60

Teaching everyone the rules is like practicing the right plays before a game so nobody accidentally cheats or makes a costly mistake.

### Question 61

If a customer does not show up, you write 'did not show up' — you do not pretend they came in and got served.

### Question 62

An attestation is like signing your name to say 'I promise this is true and complete.'

### Question 63

Charging for something the chart shows never happened is the clearest way to make a false claim.

### Question 64

If the work really happened but the note is missing, the person who did it writes the missing note the right way before you send the bill.

### Question 65

Lying on an official record can get both the company and the person who lied in serious trouble, even if someone catches it early.

### Question 66

Even if a patient really wants help paying, you cannot change the doctor's diagnosis to trick the insurance — that is still lying on the record.

### Question 67

Helping the team play by the rules means following them, learning them, and telling a leader when something looks wrong.

### Question 68

A phantom encounter is like inventing a customer who never walked in so you can charge for a visit that never happened.

### Question 69

Using your own log-in and signing only your own work is like each player keeping their own scorecard — everyone is accountable for what they wrote.

### Question 70

If you know a bill is wrong, sending it anyway makes you part of the problem and can get you in trouble too.

### Question 71

If every single note looks like a photocopy with only the name changed, something is probably not real — real visits look different from each other.

### Question 72

Write down exactly what the caller said and when, like taking a clear phone message — do not add your own guesses about what is wrong.

### Question 73

A typo, a wasteful habit, and deliberate cheating all need fixing, but only cheating needs a serious investigation — like the difference between a spilled drink, a wasteful habit, and stealing.

### Question 74

If you are not sure something really happened, you check before you charge — you do not guess and hope for the best.

### Question 75

You can fix a bill by sending a new corrected one, but a diary entry is fixed by crossing out and noting the change, not by tearing the page out.

### Question 76

The doctor is the one who figures out what is wrong; the assistant writes down what the doctor says and keeps the paperwork straight.

### Question 77

Investigators check whether the bill matches what really happened — not how nice the office looks or how happy patients said they were.

### Question 78

A late entry is the honest way to say 'I am adding this note now about something from earlier' instead of pretending you wrote it at the time.

### Question 79

If someone pressures you to do something wrong, the safe move is to say no and tell a trusted leader, not to go along and hope it stays secret.

### Question 80

When someone checks whether a bill is honest, they look at the receipt — the medical record — to see if what was charged really happened.

### Question 81

Keeping records honest means writing things down while they are fresh and checking your work, not guessing or putting it off.

### Question 82

If the label on the box does not match the recipe, you fix the label to match the recipe — you do not rewrite the recipe or leave the wrong label for more money.

### Question 83

You can be responsible for sending a false bill if you ignored obvious warning signs, even if you did not mean to cheat.

### Question 84

Write down what really happened, clearly and completely — that is the whole job of good note-taking.

### Question 85

Everyone who helps make the bill should know the rules, because their daily choices decide whether the bill is honest.

### Question 86

If you accidentally charge someone twice, you fix it and give the extra money back — you do not keep it or move it around.

### Question 87

Objective means writing the numbers and facts you can see or measure, not your opinions about a person.

### Question 88

If every patient's note is the same copy-paste, it looks like nobody really looked at the patient — like turning in the same homework for every class.

### Question 89

You cannot finish someone else's homework by making up the answers — only the person who did the work can write what they really found.

### Question 90

The whole rule in one sentence: tell the truth on the records, never fake anything, and speak up if something looks wrong.
